title: Can the smallest angle be forty five or seventeen?
description: Two possible smallest angles, forty five degrees and seventeen degrees, are tested against the full turn. Each is divided into three hundred sixty to see if it fits a whole number of times. The check lays steps round a circle.
teaching_notes: One idea: a smallest angle must fit a whole number of times into 360 degrees, so it must divide 360 exactly. Watch for students who say yes to any angle that is a whole number.

source: Figure it Out Q6 (section 9.2, second block)
video_script.why: The child decides if forty five and seventeen degrees can be the smallest angle of symmetry by dividing 360 by each.
video_script.substitution: steps of the smallest angle laid round a circle of 360 degrees, the way the book builds its lists
video_script.anchor: a circle of three hundred sixty degrees with equal steps laid round it
video_script.payoff_line: Forty five degrees can be the smallest angle, and seventeen cannot

final_answer.spoken: forty five degrees can be the smallest angle, and seventeen cannot

maths_rules: the smallest angle of symmetry must fit a whole number of times into 360°
360 ÷ 45 = 8, since 45 x 8 = 360; so 8 equal arms 45° apart work
17 x 21 = 357 and 17 x 22 = 374; 360 is not a multiple of 17, so 360 ÷ 17 is not a whole number
check: 45° x 8 = 360° lands on the full turn; steps of 17° go from 357° to 374° and miss 360°
video_script.design: A circle of three hundred sixty degrees with equal steps laid round it. Steps of forty five degrees land on the full turn. Steps of seventeen degrees pass over it.

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find if a figure can have each smallest angle.

beats.on_screen: rule: the smallest angle must fit a whole number of times into 360°, so 360° ÷ smallest angle is a whole number

marks.whole: the words whole number are underlined

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step one, the full turn is always an angle of symmetry.
<bookmark mark='whole'/>The smallest angle must fit a whole number of times into three hundred sixty.

beats.on_screen: 360° ÷ 45° = 8, a whole number, because 45° x 8 = 360°; 8 equal arms 45° apart

marks.arms: eight equal arms appear round the dot, 45° apart

narration: <bookmark mark='div'/>Step two, three hundred sixty divided by forty five is eight.
<bookmark mark='arms'/>That is a whole number, so eight equal arms, forty five degrees apart, give such a figure.

beats.on_screen: 17° x 21 = 357°, 17° x 22 = 374°; 360° is between them, so 360° ÷ 17° is not a whole number

marks.gap: 360° is marked between 357° and 374° and is circled

narration: <bookmark mark='mul'/>Step three, seventeen times twenty one is three hundred fifty seven.
Seventeen times twenty two is three hundred seventy four.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>Three hundred sixty lies between them, so seventeen does not divide three hundred sixty.

beats.on_screen: check: steps of 45° land on 360°; steps of 17° go from 357° to 374° and miss 360°

marks.land: steps of 45° are laid round the circle and the last one lands on 360°, ticked
marks.miss: steps of 17° are laid round the circle and the last one passes 360°, crossed

narration: <bookmark mark='land'/>Step four, check by laying steps round the circle.
Steps of forty five degrees land exactly on three hundred sixty.
<bookmark mark='miss'/>Steps of seventeen degrees pass three hundred sixty without landing on it.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>Forty five degrees can be the smallest angle, and seventeen cannot.
